#57945. World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

📅 14 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (844 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.
  • Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles.
  • The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World.

Conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

It has been revealed that the researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

Operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an important objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero.

In a recent development, to make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

Recent findings suggest that "In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," notes Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

It has been revealed that the researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

Recent findings suggest that "Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

According to recent reports, "This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," notes Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware.

The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

In a recent development, that capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen claims.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent

LangSmith is closed-source and restricts self-hosting to enterprise licenses, teams that run their own LLMOps stack and want to keep traces on their own servers need an alternative. To find the best fit, we set a baseline by tracing a small TypeScript agent (equipped with two tools) in LangSmith Cloud. Then, we ran the exact same agent through Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Opik, and AcruxCore using each platform's recommended TypeScript setup. All tests were run on November 5, 2026, and we pulled every trace back through each tool's API to verify the data.

According to recent reports, all four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree for the test prompt: a single agent span containing three LLM calls and two tool calls. The real differences between them come down to how much boilerplate code you have to write, how spans are typed, whether costs are tracked, and the overall server footprint.

Why Teams Look for a LangSmith Alternative.

In a recent development, langSmith remains the best choice if you already use LangChain and allow cloud hosting—it required just 25 lines of code in our test. The alternatives below are for teams that don't fit that profile.

To test these platforms, we built a simple customer support agent equipped with two tools:.

Both tools use static fixture data to ensure every test run is identical. The agent runs a standard loop: it prompts the model, executes any requested tools, and stops once the model provides a final answer.

We tested the agent with three specific prompts to see how the tracing handled different levels of complexity:.

For our comparison, we focused entirely on the third question because it generates a robust, multi-step trace.

Sources indicate that under the hood, the agent uses the standard openai package to call the qwen3.8-flash model. We originally picked this model based on its reliable tool-calling behavior during early probing thought it once skipped a tool call later.

Industry observers note that we used LangSmith as our baseline. By tracing the agent there first, we created a checklist of every field it captured, and we judged all the alternatives against that exact list.

For setup, we followed the recommended TypeScript approach from each tool's documentation. Phoenix didn't have specific instructions for using its register() helper with OpenAI in TypeScript, so we adapted the pattern from their Anthropic guide.

All five SDKs shared one package.json.

Sources indicate that here is the agent with no tracing. Each tool section adds one tracing file that imports these files and changes nothing in them.

run-plain.ts runs all three questions:.

It has been revealed that langSmith traces the plain openai package with two helpers. wrapOpenAI records each model call, and traceable records your own functions. Without traceable on the run and the tools, wrapOpenAI alone gave three separate root runs and no tool runs.

This file adds 25 lines and removes 3, and installs one package.

Industry observers note that langSmith showed one root run with five children in call order: LLM, get_order_status, LLM, get_refund_policy, LLM. Every field it recorded became a row of the checklist table under "Results". Cost appeared only after a custom price entry. In our error run the failing tool was marked as an error, but the root stayed success: traceable turned the throw into a rejected promise that our agent did not await, so the agent carried on and answered.

Recent findings suggest that langfuse self-hosts as six containers, including ClickHouse, a column store built for large scans. In our measurement the stack held 2.60–2.64 GiB of memory at idle. Its Docker Compose guide recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 16 GiB RAM, with about 100 GiB of disk.

Recent findings suggest that the TypeScript path is built on OpenTelemetry. You start the OTel Node SDK with LangfuseSpanProcessor, wrap the client with observeOpenAI, and wrap your own functions with observe:.

This file adds 31 lines and removes 5, and installs four packages. We pinned the OTel Node SDK to 0.223.0, because @langfuse/otel 6.1.1 does not accept 0.300.0.

It has been revealed that langfuse successfully recreated the same trace tree, neatly tagging the spans as AGENT, GENERATION, and TOOL. It captured all the essentials: tool calls, tool definitions, and the complete message history. However, for the LLM output, it only saved the assistant's message—dropping the finish_reason, response ID, and the provider name.

We ran our deployment in Langfuse v4's events_only mode, which turns off the v1 trace endpoint. Because of this, the API didn't return a centralized trace object or root-level sums for tokens and costs, even though the UI calculated and displayed them perfectly (we didn't test other modes).

It has been revealed that costs showed up exactly as expected once we added a custom price entry. Since Langfuse calculates prices based on the specific usage types you define, and we only set rates for input and output, the separate reasoning tokens went unpriced. Finally, during our error test, the observe wrapper let the error bubble up to the agent, correctly flagging both the tool and the root span as an ERROR.

Phoenix self-hosts as two containers, one Python server and Postgres. In our measurement it held 0.47 GiB at idle. Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, so it is not open source. Authentication is off until you turn it on.

Industry observers note that the TypeScript path uses Phoenix's register() helper and the OpenInference instrumentation for the OpenAI package. OpenInference is a set of OpenTelemetry attribute names for LLM spans. traceAgent and traceTool wrap the run and the tools:.

This file adds 32 lines and removes 3, and installs three packages.

It has been revealed that phoenix rebuilt the same tree, typed as AGENT, LLM and TOOL. Each LLM span keeps the full OpenAI response object, plus the messages as flattened attributes. The root span stores no token count, but Phoenix computes a sum for the root and the trace when you read it. Cost and those sums are only in the GraphQL API and the UI, and the REST API has no per-trace endpoint.

According to recent reports, cost appeared after a custom price entry under Settings > Models, and Phoenix priced the reasoning tokens by falling back to the output price. In the error run, the tool span and the root were marked ERROR, and the tool span carried an exception event with the stack trace.

Recent findings suggest that opik self-hosts as eight containers, including ClickHouse, MySQL and ZooKeeper. In our measurement it held 3.69 GiB at idle, the most of the four. The self-hosted UI opened without a login, so every trace was readable from any machine that could reach the port.

Industry observers note that the TypeScript path wraps the client with trackOpenAI and your own functions with track. By default trackOpenAI starts a newly introduced trace for every model call, so the file passes the run's span through the documented parent option:.

This file adds 33 lines and removes 5. It installs opik-openai 2.2.142, and npm adds opik 1.11.14 as its peer, because opik-openai asks for opik ^1.8.61.

Opik successfully recreated the trace tree, and its trace object neatly tallies token counts across all LLM spans. In the logs, tool arguments are bundled into an array, and the LLM output only retains the assistant's message.

Sources indicate that we did notice a quirk with the documented OpenAI wrapper (tested on the npm package opik 1.11.14): it tags model calls as general rather than llm, which incorrectly leaves the llm_span_count at zero. (We didn't test newer Opik core versions to see if this has changed). Additionally, because our synchronous tools execute in under a millisecond, they log the exact same start time as the subsequent LLM call, causing the UI to list the LLM call first out of order.

Sources indicate that cost tracking is entirely manual. Opik showed no costs by default, and the documentation doesn't mention a custom price table. We checked the configuration tabs on our 2.2.52 instance (Feedback definitions, AI Providers, Workspace preferences) and found no model pricing settings. To see costs, you have to manually assign a price to each individual span yourself—only the spans we hardcoded this way displayed a cost.

Sources indicate that finally, error reporting is highly detailed. If something fails, Opik attaches an error_info block—complete with the error type, message, and full traceback—directly to the tool span, the root span, and the overall trace.

AcruxCore self-hosts as five containers: Postgres, Redis, a Node API and worker, and nginx. In our measurement it held 0.39 GiB at idle, the least of the four. Its quickstart leaves sign-up open and ships a committed default GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which encrypts stored provider keys; replace it. We tested a local build from 2026-09-17.

Sources indicate that the TypeScript path AcruxCore's docs put first is its gateway. The official openai client keeps working: you point its baseURL at ACRUXCORE_BASE_URL + "/gateway" and call a model registered in AcruxCore, which forwards each call to an OpenAI-compatible provider. The gateway records every model call as an llm span. The SDK's step helpers add the rest: traces.step opens the agent span, traces.wrap wraps each tool, and two headers file the gateway's spans under the agent span:.

According to recent reports, this file adds 30 lines and removes 5, and installs one package. It builds its own client, so it does not use provider.ts. The gateway refused our team API key, so the client uses a gateway virtual key created in the dashboard.

According to recent reports, on this path every model call passes through the AcruxCore server, which none of the other four tools need. If you do not want a proxy in the request path, the SDK's register() helper sends OpenTelemetry spans from your process instead. On that path the step helpers do not join the openai package's spans, so you write the agent and tool spans by hand.

Recent findings suggest that acruxCore rebuilt the same tree, typed as agent, llm and tool, in call order. Each LLM span keeps the full response, the provider and the cached-token count, and the trace carries a token total. The LLM spans do not keep the tool definitions sent to the model, and no reasoning-token count was recorded. The trace took its name from the question, not from the agent span, and each LLM span is named by its start time.

Cost appeared on every LLM span and as a sum on the trace, from the custom price we set on the model in AcruxCore's model list. In the error run, the step helpers marked the tool span and the agent root as error with the error message, with no status code of ours. The API returned no stack trace.

Recent findings suggest that all five tools accept traces over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry wire format. trace-otel.ts sends the same spans with no vendor package: the OTel Node SDK, the OTLP/HTTP protobuf exporter and the OpenInference OpenAI instrumentation. The exporter reads its endpoint and headers from environment variables:.

We ran the two-tool question once per backend and changed only environment variables: the endpoint, the headers, and for Phoenix a resource attribute that sets the project name (without it, spans go to a default project). "Accepted" means the exporter reported success, which it does only for an HTTP 2xx, and we read the spans back through each API.

Industry observers note that opik stored the root and tool spans as general although AGENT and TOOL kinds were sent; the cause is Not tested. LangSmith mapped AGENT to its chain type. If you instrument with plain OTel and OpenInference attributes, your raw spans are not tied to one vendor, but span types, cost and trace views still differ by backend.

The first table covers setup: how much server each tool needs, how much code we changed in the agent, and how cost and the plain OTel exporter worked. Phoenix and AcruxCore had the smallest servers, and AcruxCore needed the fewest lines among the self-hosted tools. Opik was the only one without a price table.

In a recent development, the second table checks each trace against what LangSmith recorded for the same run, one field at a time. All five rebuilt the same tree with tokens and durations. They differ in span types, how much of the LLM output they keep, where token sums live, and how much detail they store for the failing tool.

Token totals for the two-tool question ranged from 1,910 to 2,111. Each tool traced a separate run and reasoning length varies, so these numbers do not compare the tools.

All five tools successfully traced our test agent, so the right choice really comes down to your team's specific constraints, infrastructure preferences, and how tracing fits into the rest of your MLOps tooling.

Sources indicate that all four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree. The real deciding factors are boilerplate code, span typing, cost tracking, and server bloat.

LangSmith remains the simplest option for LangChain people who can utilize the cloud. Otherwise, your choice depends on your priorities: Langfuse for community size, Phoenix for a lightweight Postgres footprint, Opik for strict Apache-2.0 compliance with deep error logging, or AcruxCore for combined tracing and tool governance on minimal hardware. Best of all, if you stick to standard OpenTelemetry spans, you aren't locked in—you can try them all and easily pivot later.

Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected

📅 15 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance.
  • It has been revealed that low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern.
  • These years are especially crucial because the brain is still developing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and says the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

It has been revealed that low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

These years are especially crucial because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Sources indicate that researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing.

The results indicated that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Highlighted Different Links in Girls and Boys.

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Recent findings suggest that among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

In a recent development, the researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

By contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

Sources indicate that "Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect.

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

The results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

Researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a latest way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand.
  • That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria.
  • One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a latest way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

Light Powers and Steers the Tiny Robots.

One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

For the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an notable part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

Recent findings suggest that the latest control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

Nanorobots Act as "Microscopic Cleaners".

It has been revealed that "In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," says Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices.".

It has been revealed that the robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

In a recent development, under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible.".

Recent findings suggest that the robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta has warned that it could pull WhatsApp and other encrypted services from Canada if the government moves forward with a controversial surveillance law.

The tech giant is pushing back against Bill C-22, also known as the Lawful Access Act, which would require technology companies to provide authorities with greater access to information during criminal investigations.

According to Canada’s state broadcaster, Meta representatives raised concerns during a Canadian Senate committee hearing on November 16, arguing that the proposed legislation could compromise users’ privacy and security.

Meta’s director of privacy and public policy, Robyn Greene, warned lawmakers that complying with the bill while maintaining secure, end-to-end encrypted communications would not be “technically feasible.”.

When asked whether Meta could withdraw services such as WhatsApp from Canada, the company’s head of Canadian public policy, Rachel Curran, mentioned it would have to “review all of our options.”.

She confirmed that withdrawing services would be something Meta would have to consider.

Bill C-22 would make it easier for Canadian police and intelligence agencies to access people’s information, while also allowing the government to secretly order tech companies to make certain technical changes. These could include installing surveillance-related equipment, developing tools to help authorities access data, and storing metadata about people’ communications.

Meta fears these changes could weaken encryption and put the privacy of Canadians using services like WhatsApp at risk.

Although the Canadian government has amended the legislation to strengthen encryption protections, Meta argues the changes do not go far enough.

“They have protected just the core and not the outside layers that are an integral part of the encryption process,” Curran explained.

The government, meanwhile, maintains that the legislation would not force companies to create encryption backdoors or give police unrestricted access to private messages.

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion after Facebook misled users about data privacy.

Canada could restrict Roblox & Minecraft for under 16s as part of social media ban.

Meta could remove Instagram and WhatsApp in Upcoming Mexico amid legal battle over teen safety.

According to recent reports, meta isn’t alone in its opposition. Encrypted messaging platform Signal has also warned that it would leave Canada rather than compromise its consumers’ security, while Apple has expressed concerns about the potential privacy risks.

According to recent reports, this isn’t the first time Meta has considered removing its services over a legal dispute. Earlier in 2026, the tech giant warned it could withdraw Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp from Fresh Mexico amid a legal battle over child safety.

Canada has also been considering separate restrictions on social media access for users under 16.

For now, WhatsApp remains available in Canada, and Meta has not announced any aims or a timeline for shutting down the service.

Bill C-22 has already passed the House of Commons but remains under consideration in the Senate, where lawmakers could introduce further amendments before it becomes law.

Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information.
  • It has been revealed that the challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials.
  • The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

It has been revealed that the challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

"Biology and electronics are different domains," said Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely fresh materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed.".

Building a Low Power Memory Device.

In a recent development, using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

In a recent development, that ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," mentioned Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

It has been revealed that "Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives.".

Engineering DNA to Conduct Electricity.

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

It has been revealed that this technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

Sources indicate that synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

Sources indicate that according to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

Industry observers note that "We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform.".

DNA and Perovskite Work Better Together.

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

The researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

The carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

The researchers also reported that the upcoming system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

Sources indicate that "Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane stated. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power.".

A New Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics.

The team now intends to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

Sources indicate that "Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel noted. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible.".

In a recent development, in addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

Industry observers note that the U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

Sources indicate that materials provided by Penn State. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A South Carolina business owner is suing Meta for $75,000 after the company’s security systems reportedly mistook its own AI assistant for a hacker and suspended his Facebook accounts.
  • Rather than handling the dispute himself, the man turned to the same AI assistant that triggered the suspension, which helped him prepare a lawsuit against the manufacturer responsible for creating it.
  • The unusual legal dispute comes as Meta continues expanding its AI technology, including Muse, an assistant designed to handle tasks on behalf of people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A South Carolina business owner is suing Meta for $75,000 after the company’s security systems reportedly mistook its own AI assistant for a hacker and suspended his Facebook accounts.

Rather than handling the dispute himself, the man turned to the same AI assistant that triggered the suspension, which helped him prepare a lawsuit against the manufacturer responsible for creating it.

The unusual legal dispute comes as Meta continues expanding its AI technology, including Muse, an assistant designed to handle tasks on behalf of people. The case involves a business owner who had been using the technology to manage his company’s social media presence before losing access to his accounts.

According to a November 17 report from 404 Media, Joe Thomas, who owns South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops, had been using Meta’s Muse AI agent, which he named “Baby Mia” after his granddaughter, to help run his business.

The assistant handled various responsibilities, including writing emails, creating advertisements, and producing AI-generated videos for the firm’s Facebook pages.

However, after Thomas granted Baby Mia access to his business accounts, Meta’s automated security systems reportedly identified the AI’s activity as suspicious and disabled the pages.

Thomas mentioned the suspension lasted approximately one week, preventing him from receiving fresh business inquiries through Facebook advertising.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” he told 404 Media.

“Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”.

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion after Facebook misled owners about data privacy.

Meta’s AI can now make phone calls you don’t want to make.

Meta responds after Muse AI gave stranger YouTuber’s home address on Facebook Marketplace.

According to the report, Baby Mia contacted numerous organizations and government officials while attempting to restore Thomas’s accounts.

Those efforts included contacting the FBI, Federal Trade Commission, Federal Communications Commission, Better Business Bureau, California Attorney General, and multiple attorneys. The assistant also contacted lawmakers, arranged a call with Senator Tim Scott’s office, and faxed the White House.

Thomas said the AI sent more than 100 emails during the dispute, while he personally sent none.

Industry observers note that the assistant’s efforts eventually reached Scott’s office, which provided a Privacy Act release allowing staff to assist Thomas with recovering his accounts. The document reportedly listed Baby Mia as an AI assistant who should receive updates about the case.

After the senator’s office became involved, a Meta employee contacted Thomas, and he regained access to his Facebook accounts.

Despite recovering them, Thomas is continuing with his lawsuit, which was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on November 16.

The complaint alleges that the suspension cost his business at least $25,000 in lost work, although he is seeking $75,000 in damages.

While Thomas credits Baby Mia with preparing the lawsuit and pursuing the legal action, he personally signed the court documents.

“I wouldn’t be sitting here talking to you right now if it wasn’t for what she was doing because I have not sent out one email at all and she has sent over 100,” Thomas explained.

He also said the AI made it possible for him to pursue legal action without spending thousands of dollars on legal assistance.

“There’s just no way I could have written this up, I wouldn’t have even known what to do,” he said.

According to recent reports, “Now people like me get the chance to defend ourselves in court without spending thousands of dollars to do it when we get stepped on by the big tech companies. Before AI, nobody in my position would have ever, ever thought about suing or even known how to do it, and I wouldn’t have done it, either.”.

The lawsuit remains unresolved, and it is unclear whether Thomas will receive any compensation from Meta.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.
  • The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.

The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence. Such capabilities could become increasingly key as NASA pursues missions farther from Earth, including lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions, and future human exploration.

Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. FALCON offers an alternative by allowing spacecraft to determine where they are using what they can observe around them.

According to recent reports, the FALCON payload is a joint flight experiment developed by NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive's Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling's cameras and an onboard catalog of known satellites. Together, these tools enable GPS-independent navigation while also helping the spacecraft track activity and objects in its surroundings.

"FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation," mentioned Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program at NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley. "The number of 'firsts' from Starling just keeps growing.".

Using Satellites and Debris as Reference Points.

In a recent development, the FALCON demonstration evaluated two related capabilities using Starling's onboard star tracker cameras. These cameras are standard spacecraft instruments that detect bright objects in space and help determine a spacecraft's orientation and position.

During position, navigation, and timing experiments, FALCON identified objects seen by Starling's cameras, including other spacecraft and orbital debris, and compared them with a publicly available catalog of known space objects maintained by the U.S. Department of War. Once the observed objects were identified and verified, FALCON used them as reference points to calculate Starling's orbit.

A separate set of experiments tested whether the spacecraft could improve orbital estimates for the objects it observed. Mission controllers loaded a catalog containing approximately 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.

Over a period of three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without any intervention from operators on the ground.

A First for Autonomous Optical Navigation.

FALCON's ability to determine its own orbit represents a first for a spacecraft navigating with optical cameras based on its position relative to other objects in space. In separate catalog updating tests, Starling also generated better onboard predictions of object positions than those supplied by ground stations.

These abilities could be especially valuable for future networks of satellites operating without GPS. Coordinated satellite systems may play an important role in supporting human activities on the surfaces of the Moon or Mars.

Industry observers note that precise spacecraft positioning is also essential for distributed science missions, where measurements collected from several locations in space must be accurately aligned. For space traffic management, autonomous navigation and onboard catalog updates could reduce dependence on ground-based tracking networks while improving collision avoidance.

From University Research to Commercial Technology.

According to recent reports, the FALCON experiment also demonstrates NASA's role in helping university research develop into commercial technology. The work began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project before developing into EraDrive, which is now commercializing its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.

Starling gave the technology an opportunity to be tested under real conditions in orbit, demonstrating how advanced flight software can allow satellites to function as increasingly autonomous navigators.

Later this year, Starling, which released in 2023, will expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission's four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use those combined observations to refine their positions collectively.

NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley leads the Starling mission. NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program, based at Ames and within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the Starling mission.

IBM quantum computer solves classically intractable problem in 15 minutes

📅 30 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists used a newly introduced error correction strategy to encode 70 logical qubits and tackle a problem considered classically intractable.
  • The quantum computation was completed in about 15 minutes, while leading classical computing methods would require an impractical amount of time to perform the same task.
  • IBM and researchers at the University of Chicago have announced a quantum computing demonstration that meets key criteria for quantum advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists used a newly introduced error correction strategy to encode 70 logical qubits and tackle a problem considered classically intractable.

The quantum computation was completed in about 15 minutes, while leading classical computing methods would require an impractical amount of time to perform the same task.

IBM and researchers at the University of Chicago have announced a quantum computing demonstration that meets key criteria for quantum advantage. The experiment performed a calculation beyond the practical reach of leading classical simulation techniques while also providing evidence that the quantum computer produced a reliable result.

Sources indicate that in a latest paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers describe how they achieved both goals using a newly designed form of encoded quantum circuit. The work represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing reported so far.

The circuits and experimental results have also been made publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.

Why Quantum Results Are So Difficult to Verify.

Researchers have long used a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS) to explore whether quantum computers can outperform conventional machines.

In simplified terms, RCS challenges a quantum computer to generate patterns that become so complicated that a classical computer cannot efficiently reproduce them. That makes the benchmark useful for testing the limits of classical simulation.

But it also creates a major problem. Once the quantum calculation becomes too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, verifying that the quantum machine actually produced the correct result becomes increasingly difficult as well. Eventually, checking the answer can itself become infeasible unless researchers make strong assumptions about how the quantum computer behaves internally.

The IBM and University of Chicago team approached this verification problem by developing a more structured alternative to RCS.

The researchers highlighted that their method preserves the same computational hardness criteria associated with RCS, meaning the problem remains extremely difficult for classical computers. At the same time, the added structure allows errors to be detected during the quantum computation.

"Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," mentioned Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem.".

Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers.".

70 Logical Qubits With Lower Error Rates.

The experiment also included one of the world's largest-known demonstrations of quantum error correction.

In a recent development, the researchers operated 70 logical qubits. Unlike individual physical qubits, logical qubits are encoded in a way that helps protect quantum information from errors and noise.

Using those logical qubits, the team carried out 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates," two measures that reflect the complexity of the quantum circuit.

It has been revealed that the encoded design significantly improved reliability. Effective logical error rates were 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates, allowing the circuit to maintain unusually high fidelity even while performing a large number of quantum operations.

IBM Notes Quantum Advantage Has Entered a Newly introduced Stage.

"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a latest foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically.".

The researchers found that many leading classical simulation methods would face prohibitive runtimes when attempting the same task.

The IBM quantum computer, by comparison, completed the computation in approximately 15 minutes.

A Step Toward Larger, More Trustworthy Quantum Computers.

It has been revealed that speed alone is not enough for quantum computing to become useful at larger scales. Researchers also need ways to suppress errors and establish confidence that a quantum system produced a valid result.

This experiment advances both goals at once by combining large-scale logical quantum computing with a method for evaluating the reliability of a calculation that is already beyond practical classical simulation.

Error correction and trustworthy verification are considered essential for scaling quantum computers toward more difficult problems, making the new demonstration an important step toward that goal.

Fiona, the viral hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, is now under a constant 24-hour medical watch after she ate a knitted hat that fell into her enclosure.

When you go to the zoo, there are plenty of warnings around enclosures that say don’t feed the animals or toss anything into their enclosures. If something falls in, your best bet is to ask a zookeeper to see if they can help – not to try to jump in and deal with it yourself.

Over in Cincinnati, Ohio, one zoo-goer accidentally ended up feeding Fiona the viral hippo something that isn’t in her typical diet – a knitted hat.

Industry observers note that as per CNN, the hat had been tossed up into the air from in front of the habitat and got caught by a ceiling fan. That fan then slingshotted the hat through a small one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window.

“We probably couldn’t make it happen again if we tried,” Cincinnati Zoo’s spokesperson told CNN.

They also noted that Fiona – who initially went viral for being born underweight and surviving – is getting “24-hour care and attention” as a result of the incident, which happened back on November 9.

In a recent development, “Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass it on her own,” the spokesperson added, noting that hippo was given medication and laxative-like supplements to help “push things” along. That didn’t happen, though, and they’re still waiting for the hat to come out of her body.

A device disconnects halfway through a test. The application reports a timeout, the firmware restarts, and the next attempt succeeds. Where should you start?

For developers working with connected devices, browser interfaces, or hardware prototypes, an application error is often only the final symptom. Replacing code without recording the conditions around a failure can leave you chasing the wrong layer.

This tutorial builds a small browser-based diagnostic log. It records measurements, preserves the test conditions, and exports evidence for another developer to review. You need basic HTML and JavaScript knowledge; no framework or connected instrument is required.

According to recent reports, 1. Define the question before collecting data Consider a hypothetical development board that disconnects when a peripheral starts. Several explanations remain possible: a firmware exception, a transport problem, or a power supply problem. Start with a testable question: “Does the measured supply voltage change when this peripheral starts?” That question tells you what to record and what to keep constant.

Use a known-good board of the same revision where available. Match the firmware, cable, supply, peripheral, and workload. A comparison loses value when several conditions change together.

Record the observation separately from the explanation:.

Recent findings suggest that the hypothesis remains provisional. A reading taken after the device restarts does not establish what happened during the failure.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Choose evidence that answers the question Application logs, firmware traces, and bench measurements answer different questions. A timeout establishes that an operation did not finish in time; it does not identify a failed component.

According to recent reports, for a view of specialist equipment used in phone-board troubleshooting, DIYFIXTOOL’s overview of Chip-Level Diagnostic Tools discusses thermal imaging, BGA X-ray inspection, and inductance testing. Treat it as a vendor-authored introduction to equipment categories; use instrument documentation and board-specific references when interpreting measurements.

The log below deliberately leaves interpretation to the operator. Enter a numeric value, its unit, and the conditions under which it was measured. Do not turn an isolated reading into an automatic “faulty chip” verdict.

For physical measurements, follow the board and instrument documentation and work within your training. This tutorial covers the software record rather than a procedure for probing or repairing a powered device. 3. Build a small, accessible form.

Recent findings suggest that save the following as index.html and serve it through your usual local development server. For example, if Python is installed, run python -m http. server 8000 in its directory, then open http://localhost:8000. 4. Preserve data without hiding failures.

The application stores an array of records as JSON. On reload, it parses that JSON and checks the expected field types before rendering it. Parsing alone does not validate the structure of stored data.

SitePoint’s guide to looping through JSON responses provides useful background on working with objects and arrays after parsing JSON. Each table cell uses textContent, so a note containing HTML is displayed as text rather than inserted as markup. The MDN documentation for textContent explains this behavior.

Sources indicate that storage operations sit inside try...catch blocks because browser persistence can fail. The interface keeps upcoming measurements in memory and offers an export when saving fails. It does not claim those measurements will survive a reload. For another practical vanilla JavaScript project, SitePoint’s **Markdown previewer tutorial **explores browser UI construction and persistence.

As **MDN’s localStorage documentation **explains, storage belongs to the document’s origin. Opening the application on a different port may therefore show a different log. This prototype is a single-browser tool, so export vital sessions and avoid recording customer identifiers or private device contents.

It has been revealed that 5. Compare measurements under matching conditions Suppose two hypothetical readings are 3.29 V and 3.08 V. Their difference is −0.21 V. That arithmetic is straightforward; its meaning depends on the rail specification, measurement uncertainty, workload, and timing.

According to recent reports, do not add a universal voltage threshold to the application. A device-specific limit should come from its specification or an established test procedure.

If the failure is brief, a manually entered steady-state measurement may miss it entirely. Record that limitation. The next investigation may require a time-correlated capture rather than another static reading.

When sharing a session, include the firmware revision, board revision, instrument settings, and reproduction steps. A colleague should be able to repeat the comparison without guessing how the reading was obtained. 6. Verify the workflow before relying on it Try adding a decimal reading and a negative reading, then reload the page. Confirm that both values and their units remain intact. Enter a note containing test and check that it appears literally in the table.

Export the JSON and inspect the record count. Then simulate blocked storage and confirm that the interface reports the failure while allowing an export of the current session.

Sources indicate that for a larger application, add editable entries, instrument metadata, and explicit baseline records. A shared service would also need access controls, server-side validation, and a policy for retention. These additions should follow the needs of the diagnostic workflow.

Turn a symptom into a reproducible investigation.

It has been revealed that the finished prototype captures a useful minimum: what was measured, where, when, and under which conditions. Its value comes from preserving evidence that another person can inspect.

It has been revealed that when an application error crosses into firmware or hardware, that record helps you choose the next experiment. Repeat the failure, change one variable, and document what the latest evidence supports before deciding what to fix.

  • It has been revealed that entanglement is one of the defining phenomena of quantum physics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, future quantum computers may depend on the ability to connect widely separated modules through distributed entanglement. Until now, creating this kind of connection has generally required active control and repeated measurements. Physicists at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) have now demonstrated a fully autonomous alternative based on a "quantum bath" made from correlated particles of light.

Industry observers note that published in Physical Review X, the experiment provides the first demonstration of a prediction proposed more than 20 years ago. The approach could eventually offer a upcoming foundation for practical quantum technologies.

Connecting Distant Quantum Bits.

It has been revealed that entanglement is one of the defining phenomena of quantum physics. It allows particles or systems to share correlations that cannot be explained by classical physics. Creating distributed entanglement between physically separated qubits (quantum bits) could be important for building larger quantum computers and future quantum networks.

Previous attempts to entangle distant qubits have generally followed one of two strategies. One method sends a single, actively controlled photon from one qubit to another. Another has each qubit emit a photon, with the two photons then matched in an effort to generate entanglement.

It has been revealed that the second approach was recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. However, it still depends on repeated measurements and post-selection, and even then, the process does not always successfully produce entanglement.

PhD student Alejandro Andrés-Juanes and professor Johannes Fink at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) worked with international collaborators to develop a different solution. Their system uses a quantum bath that automatically brings distant qubits into synchronization. In a prototype device, the researchers used a shared source of correlated light particles to entangle two separated qubits, experimentally realizing an idea that had remained theoretical for more than two decades.

Fully Autonomous Quantum Entanglement.

Recent findings suggest that quantum entanglement can take several forms. Continuous-variable entangled states can be produced efficiently and are therefore relatively accessible. They can be compared with a pendulum, whose position and momentum change continuously.

Many useful quantum technologies, however, depend on "discrete-variable" systems. These involve 'all-or-nothing' forms of entanglement that stationary qubits can use. The challenge for the ISTA team was finding a way to connect these readily available continuous forms of entanglement with the discrete forms needed for practical applications.

Recent findings suggest that "In this work, we aimed to overcome this mismatch between the readily available and the practically useful forms of entanglement," notes Andrés-Juanes. "By stabilizing the entangled states remotely, our approach is fully autonomous and requires no active control or measurement.".

A Quantum Bath Powered by Correlated Light.

Maintaining both entanglement and quantum coherence is one of the major difficulties facing quantum computing.

The researchers addressed that problem by making the qubits' surrounding environment itself responsible for producing and stabilizing entanglement.

"In our method, the quantum bath -- meaning the qubits' environment -- is the source of entanglement. It creates a latest ground state through a continuous stream of correlated photons," says Fink. "This way, the entangled qubit state is stabilized, even beyond the qubits' own 'lifetime', and remains always available as a resource for further quantum processing. This makes the approach conceptually significant.".

Because the entangled state remains available, researchers can access it whenever it is needed. That differs from temporary entanglement, which has to be used during the brief period when it exists.

Microwave Photons Keep Qubits Connected.

Sources indicate that to couple the qubits with the entangled photon source, the researchers relied on microwave photons. These low-energy light particles are especially useful for manipulating quantum information and are already central to leading superconducting-qubit technology.

Industry observers note that optical photons serve a different role and are commonly used in optics and atomic physics. They may also become crucial for carrying quantum information between distant quantum computers through fiber optics, an area that the Fink group at ISTA is also investigating.

Measuring the Hidden Quantum State.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers needed to confirm that the two qubits were actually synchronized inside the quantum bath. To do that, they used quantum tomography, a technique that reconstructs a quantum system by examining many different 'slices' of its behavior.

"Qubits can be in a superposition of states, but all these states collapse when we measure them, leaving us with a 0 or 1 state," states Andrés-Juanes.

In a recent development, quantum tomography allowed the researchers to perform measurements lasting only 20-80 nanoseconds and use those observations to investigate the qubits' underlying states. A nanosecond is one billionth of a second.

A 20-Year Prediction Becomes an Experiment.

By successfully entangling two isolated qubits through a quantum bath, the ISTA researchers created a proof-of-concept laboratory prototype for the long-standing theoretical proposal.

"We present a relatively simple method that could be scaled up to synchronize multiple distant qubits," says Andrés-Juanes.

The new approach is promising, but it is not yet as efficient as methods that actively control qubit states. "Our method currently transfers about 10% of the bath's available entanglement.".

The researchers suggest that one reason the idea took more than two decades to demonstrate is that the original theory was developed under idealized conditions that are difficult to reproduce experimentally.

"Our experiments helped us reveal several factors that may have prevented scientists from designing a functional quantum bath using a single source of correlated photons for distributed entanglement," states Fink.

Recent findings suggest that the prototype developed at ISTA could provide upcoming opportunities for quantum-optics experiments. It may also contribute to efforts to expand quantum processors and ultimately move them closer to fault-tolerant operation.

That includes Tara Harding and her employees, as they were trying to get home from Charlotte, North Carolina, to Bismarck, North Dakota.

Recent findings suggest that instead, her and two colleagues looked at rental cars before deciding to buy a $48,000 Ford Bronco. “If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she remarked. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.”.

Harding admitted it is an “insane” idea to splash out on a latest car, but the group eventually drove it from the car dealer’s showroom to Bismarck in 27 hours.

The three took turns napping they could drive home without stopping, meaning they’d see their families and not have to reschedule any appointments.

#57907. Latest Update: Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
